name: LM3478MAX_NOPB
title: LM3478 low-side N-channel MOSFET controller for boost, SEPIC and flyback converters, 2.97 V to 40 V, 100 kHz to 1 MHz
summary: The LM3478 is a fixed-frequency current-mode PWM controller that drives an external low-side N-channel MOSFET, for boost, SEPIC, flyback and similar converters. It runs from 2.97 V to 40 V, at a switching frequency set from 100 kHz to 1 MHz by one resistor, and regulates its FB pin to 1.26 V (±2.5 % over temperature). A push-pull driver with 1 A peak current drives the gate; peak current is sensed on a source resistor, with cycle-by-cycle limiting, a 343 mV short-circuit threshold, output over-voltage protection, UVLO, internal soft-start and thermal shutdown. Pulling FA/SD high shuts it down to 5 µA typical. It comes in SOIC-8 and VSSOP-8.

circuits.title: Typical high-efficiency step-up (boost) converter, 3.3 V to 5 V at 2 A
circuits.description: A boost converter taking a 3.3 V (±10 %) input up to 5 V at 2 A. The LM3478 drives the gate of Q1; the inductor charges while Q1 conducts and discharges into the output through the Schottky diode when it turns off. The 0.025 Ω resistor in the MOSFET source gives the current signal on ISEN, with a 0.01 µF capacitor across it to ground. The 60 k / 20 k divider returns the output to FB (1.26 V × (1 + 60 k / 20 k) ≈ 5 V). The 4.7 k and 22 nF network on COMP compensates the loop, and 40 k on FA/SD sets the switching frequency near 400 kHz.

circuits.title: Typical SEPIC converter, 3.0 V to 24 V in, 5 V at 1 A out
circuits.description: A SEPIC giving 5 V at 1 A from an input anywhere from 3.0 V to 24 V, above or below the output. L1 carries the input current into the switch node; the 1 µF ceramic coupling capacitor CS passes energy to L2 and the Schottky diode, and blocks DC between input and output, so the output falls to 0 V when switching stops. The 0.05 Ω source resistor gives the current signal, filtered by 1 nF on ISEN. The 60 k / 20 k divider sets 5 V at FB, 4.7 k with CC compensates the loop and 40 k on FA/SD sets the frequency.

circuits.title: Frequency adjust
circuits.description: One resistor from FA/SD to ground sets the switching frequency between 100 kHz and 1 MHz; Equation 7 and Figure 5-4 give its value.

circuits.title: Shutdown in frequency adjust mode
circuits.description: RFA sets the frequency through a small N-channel MOSFET to ground. With the MOSFET on, the part runs normally; turning it off lets the 10 k resistor pull the far end of RFA to a supply above 1.3 V, which raises FA/SD and, after 30 µs, shuts the part down. FA/SD must be kept below its 7 V absolute maximum.

circuits.title: Adding external slope compensation
circuits.description: A resistor RSL between ISEN and the top of the sense resistor adds external slope compensation: the added ramp ΔVSL is K × RSL, with K typically 40 µA, on top of the internal ramp (Equations 5, 6 and 22 to 25; Figure 6-5). A capacitor runs from the RSL end at the sense node to ground, beside RSEN.

circuits.title: Reducing IC input noise
circuits.description: An RC filter for the VIN pin: a 20 Ω resistor in series with the pin and a 0.1 µF or 1 µF ceramic bypass capacitor right at the pin. The bulk input capacitor (10 µF to 20 µF) and the inductor connect on the supply side of the resistor. It is suggested especially for inputs below 8 V.

operation.text: Fixed-frequency peak current-mode PWM. Each cycle the oscillator sets a latch that turns the external MOSFET on through DR. The voltage on ISEN (the sense resistor drop) goes to the PWM comparator, against the COMP voltage with the slope compensation ramp added; when the sensed voltage crosses it, the latch resets and the MOSFET turns off. FB goes to the inverting input of a transconductance error amplifier referenced to 1.26 V.

For about 325 ns after the latch sets, the PWM comparator is ignored so that the turn-on spike on the sense resistor cannot end the cycle; this is the minimum on-time of the electrical table. At very light or no load the energy delivered during the blanking time can exceed what the load takes; the over-voltage comparator on FB then holds the latch reset until the output falls back.
If FB rises to VFB + VOVP, DR goes low and the MOSFET is held off. Switching resumes when FB falls to VFB + (VOVP − VOVP(HYS)).

Below 7.2 V the internal circuits run straight from VIN; above it an internal LDO supplies them. When VIN crosses 7.2 V the small bias step acts on the loop like a load step, and the output overshoot can trip OVP: the part then regulates in hysteretic mode for some cycles, or stays there until the load drops or VIN leaves the threshold. The output stays in regulation. A resistor in series with VIN moves the threshold higher, and an RC filter on VIN reduces repeated crossings from ripple when VIN sits near 7.2 V.

Current-mode control is unstable above 50 % duty cycle without slope compensation. The internal ramp VSL is enough for many designs above 50 %. More slope is added with a resistor RSL in series with ISEN (Figure 6-4), about 40 µA × RSL; K depends on switching frequency (Figure 6-5). Only as much slope as needed is added: too much makes the loop behave like voltage-mode control.
A resistor RFA from FA/SD to ground sets the switching frequency from 100 kHz to 1 MHz (Equation 7, Figure 5-4); 40 kΩ gives 400 kHz typical.

A high level on FA/SD (above 1.35 V) held for more than 30 µs stops switching and puts the part in a low-current state, under 10 µA supply current (5 µA typical). FA/SD is kept below its 7 V absolute maximum. Figure 6-7 shows a MOSFET-switched pull-up that keeps the frequency resistor in place.

When the ISEN voltage exceeds 343 mV the switching frequency drops by a factor of 5 and stays there until the short is gone. This threshold covers the blanking time, during which the PWM comparator cannot end the cycle.
The part starts once VIN rises above the UVLO threshold, at the frequency set by RFA. An internal soft-start (4 ms typical) limits inrush current.

The part runs in continuous or discontinuous conduction. The design procedures assume continuous conduction (inductor current stays above zero all cycle), which is more efficient and usually quieter for EMI.

Parts are sized from four figures: the span of supply voltage, the target output, the span of load current and the switching frequency. The input supply impedance must be low enough that input current transients do not pull VIN below UVLO.

Choose the inductance from the minimum output current (Equation 11); a ripple of 30 % of the average inductor current is a common choice. The inductor is rated above the peak current of Equations 12 to 14 to avoid saturation. Higher switching frequency allows smaller inductance. The part senses the peak switch current, which equals the peak inductor current.
A divider from the output sets FB to 1.26 V (Equation 15). A 100 pF capacitor from FB to ground may be added to reduce noise.

The cycle ends when the sense voltage reaches the control signal, whose maximum is VSENSE less the ramp at that duty cycle, so the current limit falls as duty cycle rises (Figure 7-4); during the 325 ns blanking time the 343 mV short-circuit threshold applies. Set the limit about 120 % of the maximum operating peak current. Using the VSL ratio (Equation 19) avoids the overly wide range that the separate VSENSE and VSL limits give. RSEN affects loop stability, so check Equation 21 after choosing it; if RSEN is too large, add RSL (Equations 22 to 25) and iterate. RSL can also help filter noise on ISEN.

In a boost converter the diode carries the average load current, its peak current equals the peak inductor current, and its reverse voltage equals the output voltage. A low forward drop Schottky is recommended. For a SEPIC, the diode peak current matches the switch peak current, its reverse voltage is VIN + VOUT, and its average current equals the output current.

DR swings to VIN below 7.2 V and to 7.2 V above it (Figure 5-6). A logic-level MOSFET suits most designs and a sub-logic-level part very low inputs. The selection parameters are minimum threshold voltage, RDS(ON), total gate charge, reverse transfer capacitance and maximum drain-source voltage. In a boost the off-state drain voltage is about the output voltage, and VDS(MAX) must exceed it; in a SEPIC the peak is VIN + VOUT + VDIODE. Switching losses can dominate at high frequency.

The input inductor keeps the input capacitor ripple current fairly low. A good-quality 10 µF to 20 µF capacitor is chosen; below 10 µF, interaction with the source impedance, or switching noise, can disturb the part. Especially below 8 V input, a 20 Ω resistor in series with VIN and a 0.1 µF or 1 µF ceramic capacitor right at the pin form an RC filter (Figure 7-5), with the bulk capacitor and inductor on the supply side.

The output capacitor carries large ripple current and is rated for the RMS current of Equation 32 (boost) or 55 (SEPIC). Its ESR and ESL set the output ripple: surface-mount tantalum, polymer electrolytic, polymer tantalum or multilayer ceramic capacitors are recommended. For very low ripple a second LC filter stage is usually cheaper than a larger output capacitor.
A series resistor and capacitor from COMP to ground compensate the loop; application note AN-1286 (SNVA067) gives the boost procedure.

Since DR drives a ground-referenced N-channel switch, the part also runs a SEPIC, whose output can be above or below the input. L1 and L2 can be separate inductors or two windings on one core; coupled windings reduce input ripple and size. If both are on one core (L1 = L2 = L), the inductor equations hold with the inductance replaced by 2L. The series capacitor CS isolates input from output, protects against a shorted load and lets the output fall to 0 V in shutdown, where a boost output can only fall to VIN minus a diode drop. CS carries a large RMS current, is rated above the maximum input voltage, and suits lower-power designs. Raising L1 above its minimum reduces input and output ripple, with little further gain once the L1 ripple is under 20 % of its average current; raising L2 reduces output ripple.

The part runs from DC supplies including a car battery; then VIN needs protection against reverse polarity and against load-dump voltages above 40 V. Long supply wires may need extra bulk capacitance beside the normal input capacitor.

Fast current edges in the board inductance cause L·di/dt spikes that grow with output current, can radiate, and can upset current sensing, giving duty-cycle jitter; the 325 ns blanking time does not hide all of it. Keep the AC current loops (the paths whose current switches each cycle) as small as possible, and give the ground plane enough area for heat. Join PGND and AGND very close to the IC, and join all system grounds at one point. Place a ceramic input capacitor as close as possible to VIN, grounded near the ground pins. Application note AN-1229 (SNVA054) covers switcher layout.
